Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

intelligence noun

the power to understand; cleverness

also intelligent, highly intelligent, brains, intellect

classical

Cic. Inv. 2.160: intellegentia est, per quam animus ea perspicit, quae sunt (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 155
Traupman 333

intellegentia, intellegentiae f.

noun, first declension

understanding, intelligence

The power of discerning and understanding (Lewis & Short). The adjective is intellegēns.

Other words

  • ingenium, ingeniī n. — natural ability, cleverness, wit

    noun, second declension · also used · classical

    Inborn talent and quickness of mind, as against learning (see ability). Its first sense is a person’s nature or character (Lewis & Short).

  • intellegēns, intellegentis — intelligent, understanding; a good judge

    adjective, third declension (participle of intellegō) · also used · classical · Cic. Brut. 49 (by chapter): semperne vulgī jūdicium cum intellegentium jūdiciō congruit? (Lewis & Short); Traupman 155; Traupman 333

    Of a person who understands a matter; as a noun, an expert, a connoisseur (Lewis & Short). For a quick or clever person see clever.

  • intellēctus, intellēctūs m. — understanding, intellect

    noun, fourth declension · also used · classical · Traupman 333

    First perception by the senses (Pliny), then understanding (Quintilian, Seneca).

Examples

  • intellegentia est, per quam animus ea perspicit, quae sunt

    intelligence is the power by which the mind sees clearly the things that areCic. Inv. 2.160 (Lewis & Short)

  • manent ingenia senibus, modo permaneat studium et industria

    the old keep their wits, as long as they keep their interest and their diligenceCic. Sen. 22

See also ability, clever, mind, understand, reason.
